questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The variety and quality of courses in the Informatics department, the proximity to the mountains, being able to learn a new language

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I got a lot of information from TUM via email prior to arrival and also received a letter to my German address with some information and my student card.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a welcome meeting for all incoming exchange students. I also signed up for the Minga mentor program which I would highly recommend.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Finding housing in Munich is difficult but not impossible. Start early (2-3 months in advance) and be flexible with the move in and out dates. WG-Gesucht is a great platform for finding rooms and apartments. If you have the opportunity, going to Munich before the semester begins to look at WGs is also recommendable (a lot of them do interviews) but not a must.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Munich is a great city and I was happy to live there and not in Garching (where the Informatics department is) but it is entirely up to your preferences. Getting around with public transportation and/or bike is easy - the TUM campus in Garching is at the end of the U6 metro line so having a good connection to that is nice. Living in a WG (shared flat) is common and a great way to get to know new people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Quite straight-forward. You sign up for courses in TUMonline (like KUnet). It is a lot more flexible than at KU in the way that you can register for as many courses as you like and then deregister (or just not register for the exam - that is a separate process but TUM will remind you of that and help you) for those that you do not want to take. For seminars and practical courses, you have to submit an application some months before the semester begins - you will receive information and guidance about this from TUM. Language courses also have their own registration process but are really nice.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The people working in the administration are willing to help but also quite busy during peak periods. I asked my mentor about a lot of things i.e. recommendations for courses.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful - I got all the classes that I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Register for more courses than you need to take, check them out during the first week or two and then decide which ones you want to keep. 30 ECTS in Informatics can be a lot at TUM so try to balance it with some language courses or courses from other departments.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: High level, professors and PhD students are generally very committed and available, writing papers (and potentially trying to publish them) is quite common so ask your professor if you are interested in that. I really enjoy attending a seminar and a practical course as opposed to only taking "regular" courses (lectures + exercises).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Lectures were quite similar. Some of them were partly taught by PhD students and it actually worked really well because they lectured about their current research. In the courses that I took, there were less assignments than I am used to at DIKU and more self-studying, reading, and doing project work (with supervision from PhDs). Seminars and practical courses are quite different - a lot of independent work, research, literature review, writing an article, presenting it etc.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Advanced NLP, Master Praktikum - Machine Learning for Natural Language Processing Applications, Master Seminar - Current Topics in Medical Machine Learning and Computational Pathology, German as a Foreign Language B1.2, Innovative Entrepreneurs - Leadership of High-Tech Organizations

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Courses from UnternehmerTUM if you are interested in innovation and entrepeneurship. Any seminar and practical course that fits your interests because the style of teaching is great and very different from lectures.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: None. Most of my "personal spendings" were spent on traveling.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Cheaper: Groceries, going out to eat or drink, public transportation (the Deutschlandsticket which allows you to use regional transportation all over Germany is great).
More expensive: Rent.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
ZHS: Sports institution for universities (like KSI). They also do hiking trips which I enjoyed a lot. Also a great way to practice German.
ENS arranges a lot of social and cultural events for Erasmus students as well as trips to nearby cities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Sports are very popular in Munich and a great way to meet people. Lots of running clubs (Deru, Adidas, NorthFace, ZHS). Going hiking in the alps on the weekends. Most museums cost 1 euro on Sundays.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go hiking! And travel with train to nearby cities like Salzburg, Vienna, Verona, Zürich, Köln etc.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I did not find the culture very different from Denmark - perhaps slightly more conservative but also more polite.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join sports clubs or yoga studios and attend events in the city. Study at cafés like Lost Weekend (many students).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The appreciation of the outdoors and going hiking. The politeness.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Try to get a spot in a seminar and a practical course - it's worth it and super interesting. 
2) Make use of all the great academic opportunities that TUM offers. Join UnternehmnerTUM in some capacity if you're interested in innovation.
3) Bring your hiking gear and go to the alps on the weekends.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not that I can think of but I would definitely recommend going!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Having more time than I am used to at home to dive into my courses (while not being stressed out) and being outside so much.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Not being able to share my everyday life with my friends and family.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
